strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: identifying environmental changes that cause pretrained robot manipulation policies to fail.

weaknesses: The central probabilistic interpretation is incorrect. Equations (7)–(8) equate the adversary's action-selection probabilities with robot failure probabilities, explicitly interpreted as P(Failure | Env) on page 7. Conditional failure probabilities across environments need not sum to one: all nine configurations could fail with probability one. PPO optimizes action selection rather than estimating these conditional probabilities. This fundamental error undermines the main quantitative results.

The entropy-based robustness conclusions are unsupported. Uniform action preferences can occur when all perturbations cause failure or when none do; concentrated preferences can reflect the optimizer selecting one of several equally failure-inducing actions. Appendix D explains softmax normalization but establishes no relationship between policy entropy and overall failure risk. The zero entropy coefficient in Appendix A also provides no incentive to preserve coverage of equally rewarding failure modes.

The evaluation does not independently validate the proposed analysis. Figures 3–6 primarily replot the same policy probabilities, without measured per-configuration failure rates, calibration tests, ranking validation, repeated-run uncertainty, or quantitative failure-discovery curves. The qualitative rollout example cannot establish accurate failure quantification or comprehensive failure discovery.

No search-method baselines substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage. The six robot policies are systems under test, not competing failure-discovery methods. Comparisons against uniform sampling, exhaustive evaluation, bandit methods, or existing stress-testing approaches under equal rollout budgets are missing. Only nine discrete perturbations are documented, despite Section 3.1 mentioning 20 actions, and no experiment demonstrates the claimed need for large-scale sequential search.

The methodological novelty is limited. The framework largely applies standard PPO with a failure reward to simulator perturbations. Its advance over the cited RL-based failure-discovery and adaptive stress-testing literature is not established through a new algorithm, theoretical result, or convincing empirical advantage.

Experimental scope and reproducibility are insufficiently specified. The manuscript omits total training budgets, evaluation trial counts, seeds, precise perturbation parameters, policy training data/checkpoints, and clear reset and episode protocols. Stacking, pushing, reaching, and language-conditioned policies are claimed, but corresponding task-specific and language-model results are not identified. These omissions prevent verification of the stated breadth and robustness conclusions.

weaknesses: The central probability estimator is mathematically invalid. Equations (7)–(8) equate the adversary’s action-selection probability with the robot’s conditional failure probability. These are different quantities: all nine configurations could cause failure with probability one, whereas the adversary’s probabilities must sum to one. PPO optimizes action preferences, not calibrated failure estimates. This invalidates the main probability-quantification claim and the interpretation of the reported plots.

The entropy-based robustness conclusions do not follow. A uniform adversary distribution is compatible with configurations that all succeed or all fail; it does not establish broad vulnerability or increased overall risk. Appendix D explains softmax properties but supplies no theoretical or empirical connection between policy entropy and robot failure rates.

The evaluation does not independently validate the method. Figures 3–6 visualize learned action probabilities rather than measured conditional failure rates. There are no reported calibration results, ranking-validation metrics, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, or quantitative per-task success rates. The illustrative rollout cannot establish the accuracy of the proposed failure analysis.

The claimed search-efficiency advantage is unsupported. The reported action space contains only nine configurations, yet there are no comparisons against exhaustive evaluation, uniform sampling, bandit methods, or existing adversarial search under matched rollout budgets. Training cost, failure-discovery curves, and ablations are absent, leaving the benefit of PPO unestablished.

Novelty is limited and insufficiently distinguished from related work. The method combines standard PPO, a standard CNN, and environmental perturbations. The paper cites existing RL-based failure discovery and stress testing but does not demonstrate a substantive methodological advance or a compelling empirical advantage over those approaches.

Experimental scope and reproducibility are inadequately specified. Section 3.1 mentions 20 actions, whereas Appendix B and the figures use nine. Exact perturbation settings, reset and sequential-intervention protocols, total training budget, evaluation trial counts, and tested-policy checkpoints are missing. Language-conditioned models and multiple tasks are claimed, but corresponding identifiable model results and task-level breakdowns are not provided.

strengths: Addresses an important robotics problem through a framework that operates without access to manipulation-policy internals and connects failure identification to policy improvement.
Experiments cover several manipulation tasks and five policy families, including diffusion policies, with an additional UR5e demonstration.

Reported pairwise ranking results are promising: PPO achieves 82.3%, 84.0%, and 76.0% on Lift, Square, and Pick Place, outperforming the tested RL alternatives. Appendix experiments also show success-rate improvements after fine-tuning on environmental variations.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic interpretation is unsound. Section III-C equates PPO action-selection probabilities with manipulation failure probabilities. These are different quantities: policy probabilities depend on shaped rewards, competing actions, and sequential returns, while conditional failure probabilities need not sum to one across perturbations. Gaussian action-density ratios likewise need not represent relative failure likelihoods. Consequently, the entropy/FSI interpretations and Figure 8's approximately uniform 'zero-failure' reference do not establish improved robustness.

The continuous-space algorithm is internally inconsistent. Algorithm 2 maps sampled actions to known embeddings and executes the manipulation policy, whereas Sections III-B and III-C describe exploration without environment changes or policy rollouts. State transitions and the source of failure labels in this latter setting are insufficiently specified. Reusing nearest-neighbor labels could support interpolation, but does not itself demonstrate active discovery of previously unknown failures.

The representation-learning objective is unclear. Labels are defined as binary success/failure outcomes, so Equation 1 attracts all examples sharing an outcome; the accompanying explanation instead describes grouping semantically similar actions. Meanwhile, Table V rewards separating every action through an identity-like similarity matrix. These are different objectives, and embedding orthogonality alone does not establish better failure prediction.

The comparisons do not establish the contribution of RL over the already supervised embedding. Missing baselines include direct failure classification, nearest-neighbor prediction, and random or adaptive testing under equal rollout budgets. Embedding ablations measure similarity structure rather than downstream diagnostic performance. No discovery-versus-budget or runtime results support the efficiency claims; the highlighted 23.3-point improvement measures pairwise ranking accuracy, not additional failures discovered.

The generalization protocol is insufficiently controlled and documented. It is unclear whether unseen perturbations are excluded from both embedding training and PPO training. Figure 3 uses rollout frames, whereas the stated diagnostic input is an initial observation, leaving inference-time information ambiguous. Results lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates, and the real-robot evaluation provides a small ranking example without trial counts or quantitative accuracy.

Fine-tuning results show that additional environmental training data can help, but do not isolate RoboMD's selection benefit. There is no equal-data, equal-compute comparison against random selection or uniformly diversified augmentation. Evaluation concentrates on Lift and table-color changes, while the procedure and cost for obtaining successful fine-tuning demonstrations remain unclear.

Reproducibility and reporting require substantial improvement. The initial rollout count M, embedding-training details, reward constants, and total training budgets are not adequately specified. Table I also reports GPT-4o's average as 33.3%, although its listed results average 44.3%. Together with the methodological ambiguities, these issues prevent confident verification of the central claims.
